questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Underlying Values of the Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The underlying values of the Constitution are the principles of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity enshrined in the Preamble, which guide the interpretation and working of the entire constitutional order.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Underlying Values of the Constitution'.
questions.a: The Constitution is not just a legal document but a moral and philosophical one, expressing the values and aspirations of the Indian people through its Preamble and provisions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Underlying Values of the Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Introduction: The Philosophy of the Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Constitutional Morality' refers to.
questions.a: Constitutional morality is the adherence to the norms and values of the constitution in public life, requiring that all institutions and individuals respect constitutional principles even when they conflict with personal or sectional interests.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Constitutional Morality'.
questions.a: Constitutional morality means that the constitution is not merely a set of rules but a moral order that must guide the behaviour of citizens, parties, and institutions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Constitutional Morality' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Constitutional Morality

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Separation of Powers' refers to.
questions.a: Separation of powers is the principle that the legislative, executive, and judicial functions of government should be kept distinct and exercised by different organs, with checks and balances among them to prevent concentration of power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Separation of Powers'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution does not follow a rigid separation of powers but provides for a functional separation with checks and balances among the legislature, executive, and judiciary.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Separation of Powers' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Separation of Powers

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Secularism' refers to.
questions.a: Secularism in the Indian context means that the state treats all religions equally, does not have an official religion, and maintains a principled distance from religion while protecting the religious freedom of all citizens.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Secularism'.
questions.a: Indian secularism is distinct from Western secularism: it does not strictly separate religion and state but engages with all religions equally to protect religious freedom and reform.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Secularism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Secularism

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fundamental Rights and Duties' refers to.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights are basic human rights guaranteed by the Constitution under Part III (Articles 12 to 35) that are enforceable by courts, while Fundamental Duties are obligations of citizens under Part IVA (Article 51A) that promote civic responsibility.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fundamental Rights and Duties'.
questions.a: The Constitution balances rights with duties: Fundamental Rights protect individual liberty and equality, while Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their obligations to the nation and society.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fundamental Rights and Duties' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Rights and Duties

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Directive Principles of State Policy' refers to.
questions.a: Directive Principles of State Policy, contained in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51), are guidelines for the state in making laws and policies, aimed at establishing social and economic justice, and are not enforceable by courts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Directive Principles of State Policy'.
questions.a: Directive Principles embody the vision of a welfare state, guiding the government to reduce inequalities, promote welfare, and secure a just social order, even though they are not legally enforceable.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Directive Principles of State Policy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Directive Principles

concepts.title: Unity and Integrity of the Nation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation' refers to.
questions.a: The unity and integrity of the nation is a constitutional value that seeks to preserve India's territorial unity and the emotional integration of its diverse peoples into a single national community.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation'.
questions.a: The Constitution promotes unity and integrity through a federal structure with a strong centre, single citizenship, provisions for emergency, and the goal of fraternity in the Preamble.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Unity and Integrity of the Nation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Democratic Values' refers to.
questions.a: Democratic values are the principles of popular sovereignty, political equality, freedom, accountability, and rule of law that underlie the democratic form of government established by the Constitution.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Democratic Values'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution is founded on democratic values, establishing a representative democracy based on universal adult franchise, free elections, and accountable government.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Democratic Values' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Democratic Values

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Justice' refers to.
questions.a: Social justice is the principle that the state should reduce inequalities of income, status, and opportunity, and ensure a fair distribution of resources and protection of the disadvantaged sections of society.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Justice'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution commits the state to social justice through Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, reservations, and provisions for the welfare of weaker sections.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Social Justice' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Social Justice

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Constitutional Identity' refers to.
questions.a: Constitutional identity is the distinctive character of the Constitution expressed through its basic structure, values, and institutions, which gives the nation its unique political and moral identity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Constitutional Identity'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution has a unique identity shaped by its commitment to democracy, secularism, social justice, federalism, and the protection of fundamental rights, distinguishing it from other constitutions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Constitutional Identity' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conclusion: Constitutional Identity
